strengths: Significance: Dataset sensitivity is an important and underexplored problem for circuit discovery; a black-box wrapper that can identify stable components would be practically useful.

Originality: Applying deletion-based randomized smoothing component-wise to circuit masks is a sensible new synthesis, even though its ingredients come directly from RS-Del and prior component-wise certification.

Evaluation breadth: The experiments cover two ResNet architectures, three component-scoring rules, and several nominal distribution shifts. The reported accuracy and sparsity improvements are large and consistent enough to motivate further investigation.
Presentation: The paper is generally clear, well organized, and visually polished. The distinction between certified-in, certified-out, and abstained components is explained intuitively.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript acknowledges computational overhead, the radius/deletion tradeoff, restriction to CNNs, and the danger of treating certified explanations as complete accounts of model behavior. No material ethical issue is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theorem: Theorem 3.1 claims invariance of the thresholded three-valued decision A_tau(D'), but the proof establishes only invariance of the binary smoothed argmax. An edited dataset can retain the same argmax while its confidence falls below tau, changing a certified-in/out decision into abstention. The last equality in the proof therefore does not establish the stated result, undermining the claimed invariant certified circuit.

Soundness—vacuous reported radius: With p_del=0.6 and tau=0.95, Equation 5 gives floor(log(0.55)/log(0.6))=1, while the theorem covers edit distances strictly less than r. Thus the experiments, as written, certify only distance zero, not one edit. This conflicts with the paper's interpretation of r as the number of allowed edits and with its broader robustness claims.

Statistical certification is incomplete: A per-vertex failure probability alpha does not yield a 1-alpha guarantee for the entire circuit. The appendix notes that simultaneous certification requires alpha/|V| and a union bound, but the experimental section instead states that all results are guaranteed using alpha=0.001, without saying that the correction was applied. The confidence-bound procedure is also insufficiently specified, particularly for both inclusion and exclusion decisions.

Evaluation validity is unclear for ImageNet-O: Standard ImageNet-O contains categories outside the ImageNet-1k label space, so class accuracy for “corresponding classes” and class-specific ImageNet circuits is not naturally defined. The paper does not explain any mapping or filtered subset, yet reports cACC as high as 98%. This makes a substantial part of the OOD evidence uninterpretable.

The empirical comparison does not isolate the proposed mechanism. Certified circuits are effectively stability-selected ensembles of 1,000 discovery runs, whereas the baseline is a single top-K circuit. Missing controls include majority/stability selection without the certificate, matched-size top-K or random-pruning baselines, and comparisons at identical sparsity. Consequently, gains cannot be attributed specifically to certification.

The paper selects peak cACC and the corresponding K separately on each OOD test set. This uses test-distribution performance for model selection and makes the headline accuracy/compactness comparisons optimistic. Structural IoU is likewise reported at the K maximizing the certified–baseline cACC gap, which is particularly favorable and confounded by circuit size.

The evaluation supports only target-class sufficiency under an oracle choice of class-specific circuit: the evaluator must know the target class before choosing the circuit. It does not assess necessity, causal faithfulness, or ordinary classification without target-label knowledge. Stability alone also does not imply that selected neurons encode the intended semantic concept, so claims of removing spurious features or “provably reflect[ing] the concept” exceed the evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate: code is only promised, and essential details are absent, including concept-dataset sizes and splits, exact class overlap/selection for each OOD benchmark, preprocessing, relevance computation, K grid, confidence-bound implementation, seeds, ablation mechanics in residual networks, runtime, and uncertainty across samples or classes.

Originality is moderate rather than high because the theoretical construction is largely a direct component-wise application of existing RS-Del and segmentation-style abstention. Given the incorrect central guarantee and the lack of a nontrivial demonstrated radius, the current manuscript does not yet validate its main claimed contribution.

Originality: Applying deletion smoothing and component-wise abstention to dataset-to-circuit mappings is a sensible new combination, even though its ingredients come directly from prior certification work.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers two ResNet architectures, three channel-scoring rules, and several distribution shifts. The reported accuracy and sparsity improvements are large, and the accuracy–size curves are more informative than reporting a single operating point.

Presentation and ethics: The high-level motivation and pipeline are easy to follow. The impact statement appropriately warns that a certificate is relative to a particular threat model and does not make a circuit a complete explanation.
weaknesses: Soundness—central theorem/proof gap: Theorem 3.1 claims invariance of the thresholded three-valued decision A_tau(D'), but the proof establishes only invariance of the binary argmax label A(D'). Its confidence at D' may fall below tau, in which case A_tau(D') abstains. The displayed conclusion therefore does not follow from the cited RS-Del result.

Soundness—no whole-circuit invariance: The theorem constrains only vertices that are non-abstaining at the original dataset. An originally abstained vertex is unconstrained and could become certified-in after an edit, changing the induced circuit. Thus even a corrected per-vertex result would not justify the repeated central claim that the returned circuit remains unchanged.

Soundness—the reported certificate is effectively vacuous: With p_del=0.6 and tau=0.95, Equation 5 gives r=1, while Theorem 3.1 applies only when edit distance is strictly less than r. This covers distance zero, not one dataset edit. The paper nevertheless describes r=1 as a meaningful edit certificate and broadly claims robustness to dataset edits.

Statistical guarantee: The main text says all results hold with confidence 1-alpha, using alpha=0.001, but does not state that the per-vertex confidence was adjusted for thousands of vertices. Appendix A merely says one can use alpha/|V| for simultaneous coverage. Without showing that this was actually done—and potentially also accounting for many classes—the claimed circuit-level confidence is unsupported.

Experimental validity: Peak cACC and its K are selected separately on each test distribution, including OOD datasets. This uses OOD labels to choose the operating point and makes the headline transfer results oracle-tuned rather than evaluation of one preselected circuit configuration. No validation protocol, uncertainty estimates, hypothesis tests, or repeated-run variability are reported.

The baseline comparison is confounded: Certification changes effective circuit size through abstention, yet the main table compares independently selected peak points rather than accuracy at rigorously matched sizes or compute. Consequently, the results show that this particular stability-based pruning heuristic can improve a weak top-K channel baseline, not that certification itself causes better mechanisms or OOD generalization.

Dataset/evaluation definitions are problematic. ImageNet-O contains categories absent from ImageNet, making the claimed evaluation of corresponding ImageNet class circuits—and an 81% full-model class accuracy—unclear under the standard benchmark definition. The paper gives no mapping or alternative protocol that could explain these numbers.

The structural-stability analysis chooses K to maximize the certified–baseline accuracy gap, which is a favorable post-hoc selection criterion unrelated to structural IoU. It also lacks matched-size controls and uncertainty or significance analysis, so it cannot substantiate convergence to an invariant semantic core.

Reproducibility is inadequate: The paper omits concept-dataset sizes and splits, the identities/mapping of the 100 classes across benchmarks, exact relevance and rank formulas, the K grid, confidence-bound implementation, multiplicity correction, sampling seeds, treatment of empty deletion samples, training/checkpoint details, and runtime. Code is only promised for future release.

Originality and scope are limited relative to the claims: The formal construction is largely a direct component-wise application of RS-Del plus an existing abstention rule, while experiments cover only coarse residual-block channels in pretrained CNNs and simple top-K heuristics. No evidence supports generalization to modern automated circuits, transformers, or genuinely causal circuit structures.

Presentation overstates the evidence: Dataset-edit stability is described as a prerequisite for and explanation of OOD generalization, but no theorem establishes that relationship. Claims that abstained neurons are spurious, harmful, or less concept-aligned are inferred from accuracy rather than tested mechanistically. The limitations section mentions computation and architectural scope but does not acknowledge the vacuous chosen radius, theorem mismatch, oracle selection, or benchmark ambiguity. These failures affect the paper’s defining contribution, warranting strong rejection rather than a revision-level score.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: circuit discovery can depend strongly on the concept dataset. Treating dataset-to-circuit stability as a certification problem is a useful framing, and applying deletion smoothing component-wise is an intuitive, potentially valuable idea. The reported empirical gains are substantial across two ResNet architectures, three scoring rules, ImageNet, and four distribution shifts. Evaluating compactness, target-class sufficiency, non-target accuracy, and structural overlap provides several complementary perspectives.

The framework is modular and nominally applicable to any circuit-discovery procedure producing component-wise binary decisions. Per-component abstention is also practically appealing because it exposes uncertainty instead of forcing every component into or out of a circuit.

The manuscript is polished and easy to follow, with effective figures and a clear high-level narrative. It acknowledges computational cost, the radius/deletion-rate tradeoff, architecture scope, and the risk of overinterpreting certified explanations. No unresolved ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: The central theorem does not establish the stated guarantee. The proof invokes RS-Del to show invariance of the binary argmax label, but concludes invariance of the thresholded three-valued decision. These are different: a vertex can have probability above τ on D, retain the same argmax on D′, yet fall below τ and therefore become abstained. No bound showing that D′ also remains above the certification threshold is provided. Consequently, invariance of the certified circuit itself—the paper's main claim—is unsupported.

The experimental certificate is effectively vacuous under the manuscript's own notation. With p_del=0.6 and τ=0.95, Equation 5 gives r=floor(log(0.55)/log(0.6))=1, while Theorem 3.1 covers dist_edit(D,D′)<r. Thus only distance zero is certified. If the intended condition is ≤r, the theorem and proof must be corrected; even then, the experiments certify only one edit, which is weak relative to the paper's motivating claims.

The confidence accounting is incomplete. The main text claims all certified results hold with confidence 1−α, whereas the appendix says simultaneous validity requires a per-vertex error α/|V| and a union bound, without stating that this correction was used. Section 3.4 also omits the actual confidence-bound decision rule, including how exclusion is certified. With thousands of channels, per-vertex rather than circuit-level coverage materially weakens the claimed guarantee.

The evaluation does not isolate the benefit of certification from that of expensive subsampling and aggregation. The proposed method runs the discovery algorithm 1,000 times, while the baseline appears to be a single top-K run. A matched stability-selection or bagging baseline, equal-size comparisons, and a compute-matched analysis are needed before attributing the accuracy gains specifically to certification.

Several evaluation semantics are insufficiently defined. A different class-conditioned circuit is selected using the target label, so cACC is a sufficiency diagnostic rather than ordinary classification performance; statements that the circuits classify OOD data or outperform the full model overstate what is measured. Moreover, ImageNet-O is described as containing categories absent from ImageNet, yet the paper evaluates 'corresponding classes' and reports class accuracy without explaining any label mapping. This makes a major part of the OOD evidence difficult to interpret.

The experiments do not directly measure the property being certified by applying bounded dataset edits and checking circuit decisions. Structural IoU instead uses large distribution shifts, and its K is chosen post hoc to maximize the certified–baseline accuracy gap, which can bias the comparison. There are no uncertainty estimates, significance tests, or robustness results across discovery samples and random seeds.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a main-track claim: the manuscript does not report concept-dataset sizes or splits, exact relevance and rank definitions, the K grid, preprocessing, model checkpoints, handling of empty deletion samples, confidence-interval implementation, per-dataset class overlap, random seeds, or runtime. Code is only promised for future release.

The interpretation that unstable components are 'spurious' and that the retained circuit better represents the underlying concept is not established by stability or sufficiency alone. Stable dataset artifacts can be certified, while semantically important but heterogeneous features can be abstained. Qualitative examples and causal or feature-semantic validation would be needed to support this central mechanistic interpretation.

Overall, the framing and empirical observations are promising, but the invalid theorem step, trivial stated radius, ambiguous confidence guarantee, and under-specified evaluation undermine both soundness and reproducibility. These are central rather than cosmetic issues, so the current version does not meet the acceptance bar despite its strong presentation and potentially significant direction.

strengths: The problem is important: dataset sensitivity is a genuine obstacle to treating discovered circuits as reliable mechanistic explanations. Applying discrete randomized smoothing at the dataset-to-circuit level is a useful and intuitively appealing direction.

The method is modular and potentially broadly applicable. It combines deletion smoothing with component-wise abstention and evaluates node-level vision circuits and edge-level language circuits across ResNet, ViT, and GPT-2.

The empirical study is broad. It includes multiple distribution shifts, three vision scoring rules, a majority-vote ablation, radius/data-size analyses, runtime measurements, and seed-stability experiments. Several reported accuracy-compactness improvements are large.

The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. The appendix provides hyperparameters, model-component definitions, sample-complexity analysis, and pseudocode. The impact statement appropriately warns that certified circuits are incomplete explanations tied to a particular threat model. weaknesses: The central theorem does not establish the stated invariance of the three-valued certified algorithm. RS-Del yields invariance of the binary smoothed argmax label. The proof concludes only that the unthresholded label satisfies A_tilde(D')=A_tilde(D); it never proves that its confidence at D' remains above tau. Consequently, a component certified in or out at D can become abstain when the thresholded procedure is rerun on D'. The claimed equality A_tilde_tau(D')=A_tilde_tau(D), and hence the repeated claim that the returned certified circuit itself remains unchanged, do not follow.

Even a corrected binary-label certificate would establish stability, not semantic correctness. A consistently selected component can encode a stable spurious correlation. Thus claims that the method 'provably reflects the concept,' is 'better aligned with the target concept,' or suppresses spurious features are stronger than the theorem supports; the qualitative activating-patch examples do not provide causal or systematic evidence for those claims.

Model selection uses the evaluation distributions. Results report peak cACC over K separately for every ID/OOD dataset, so the circuit size is selected using target-test performance. For language, Appendix B.2 additionally selects tau and deletion probability separately for each task and split by highest peak cACC, including OOD splits. This oracle tuning substantially weakens the claimed out-of-distribution transfer result; hyperparameters should be chosen without OOD labels and then frozen.

The vision ID experiment reuses the same 50 ImageNet validation images for circuit discovery and evaluation, rather than using a held-out ID set. Moreover, cACC evaluates each example using its ground-truth class-specific circuit, so it is a conditional sufficiency measure rather than ordinary predictive accuracy. Comparisons such as 94% circuit accuracy versus 7% full-model accuracy on ImageNet-A are therefore easy to misinterpret as improved deployable classification.

The ImageNet-O protocol is internally unclear. The appendix correctly describes ImageNet-O as containing categories outside ImageNet-1k, yet states that OOD evaluation uses the same 100 ImageNet classes except for OOD-CV. It is not explained how class-specific circuits, labels, and cACC are defined for semantic anomalies. This ambiguity affects a headline benchmark.

Evidence for structural stability is under-specified and partly selected post hoc: Figure 6 chooses K to maximize the certified-baseline cACC gap, reports no numerical IoU summary or statistical test, and does not clearly explain class matching for every OOD dataset. Most main language results and accuracy-size curves also lack uncertainty across datasets, prompts, or seeds.

The advertised black-box generality conflicts with the runtime claim. The approximately 2.4x cost relies on caching per-example additive scores, which need not be possible for an arbitrary circuit-discovery algorithm and is not demonstrated for EAP-IG. A general wrapper requires roughly n executions of the base algorithm.

Reproducibility is only partial. Many implementation details are supplied, but the manuscript's code field is empty, the exact sampled ImageNet classes and data-generation artifacts are not provided, and key OOD evaluation and selection procedures remain ambiguous. The limitations section honestly discusses compute, small concept datasets, and scope, but omits the theorem/abstention mismatch, oracle OOD tuning, and ID data reuse. No major new ethical risk is evident, although the language around 'certified explanations' could encourage over-trust given that only a narrow structural-stability property is targeted.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem: circuit discovery can be highly sensitive to the concept dataset. Applying deletion smoothing and component-wise abstention to this setting is a clear, potentially useful idea, even though the ingredients are largely adapted from RS-Del and certified segmentation.

The empirical study has broad surface coverage, spanning ResNets, ViT-B/16, GPT-2 Small, several scoring methods, ID/OOD datasets, and node- and edge-level circuits. Useful supplementary analyses include majority voting, seed stability, dataset-size/radius tradeoffs, runtime, and family-wise error control.

The limitations and impact sections acknowledge computational cost, dependence on concept-set size, restricted model scale, and the danger of treating a certified circuit as a complete explanation. weaknesses: The central theorem is not proved as stated. Theorem 3.1 claims invariance of the thresholded three-valued decision A_tau(D') in {in, out, abstain}. The Appendix instead invokes RS-Del to establish invariance only of the binary smoothed argmax. A perturbation can preserve the binary argmax while reducing its probability from above tau to below tau, causing the thresholded procedure to change from certified-in/out to abstain. The proof's final equality silently replaces A_tau(D') with the binary argmax. Consequently, the advertised guarantee that the returned certified circuit remains unchanged is unsupported, which is a fundamental soundness problem rather than a minor proof omission.

The experimental protocol has substantial selection leakage. Vision circuits are discovered from 50 ImageNet validation images per class and then evaluated ID on those same images. Results report the peak over K on each evaluation dataset, while the language appendix explicitly says that tau and deletion probability are selected separately for each task and split by highest peak cACC. Thus OOD test labels influence model and sparsity selection, making the reported transfer gains optimistic. Significance tests after selecting peak K also do not account for this selection.

The ImageNet-O evaluation is insufficiently defined and appears internally inconsistent. The manuscript correctly describes ImageNet-O as containing categories outside ImageNet-1k, yet states that OOD evaluation uses the same 100 ImageNet classes except for OOD-CV and reports class-specific accuracy as high as 0.98. Since ImageNet-O examples do not have corresponding ImageNet class labels or class-specific concept circuits under the stated setup, the reported cACC cannot be interpreted or reproduced without a missing mapping or a different metric.

The language certification configurations use p_del=0.99 with only 100 training prompts, so a sampled dataset is empty with probability 0.99^100, approximately 0.366. Hundreds of the 1,000 Monte Carlo samples should therefore be empty, but the base EAP-IG algorithm and its score on an empty dataset are never defined. The formal subsequence definition also assumes at least one retained element. This directly affects the large reported radii of 42–59.

The evaluation does not establish that the selected structures are mechanistic circuits in a strong causal or explanatory sense. The principal metric is class-conditioned sufficiency under zero ablation, with the correct class determining which circuit is run. Its ability to exceed full-model accuracy—even reaching 94% where the full model has 7% ImageNet-A accuracy—shows that it is not comparable to ordinary predictive accuracy and may reflect oracle class conditioning plus removal of competing logits. Necessity, completeness, intervention baselines, and known-ground-truth circuit recovery are not evaluated.

The claimed link between edit stability, removal of spurious features, and OOD generalization is asserted rather than demonstrated. Arbitrary edit distance does not encode semantic equivalence, and the main vision guarantee covers only one edit among 50 examples. Top-activating-patch montages are subjective and do not show that abstained neurons causally encode spurious cues. Moreover, Figure 6 measures empirical rediscovery under large distribution shifts that are outside the certified threat model.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the detailed appendix: the abstract's code field is blank, exact score computation and intervention details are incomplete, generated language datasets and their seeds are unavailable, the K sweep/model-selection protocol is underspecified, and the ImageNet-O ambiguity is unresolved. The impact discussion appropriately warns against false assurance, but the manuscript itself repeatedly overstates binary-label stability as invariance of the entire abstaining circuit.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: circuit-discovery results can depend strongly on the concept dataset. Treating the dataset-to-circuit mapping as the object to be certified is a useful perspective.

The proposed wrapper is algorithm-agnostic and combines deletion smoothing with component-wise abstention in a conceptually simple way. Experiments cover ResNet-50/101, ViT-B/16, GPT-2 Small, node- and edge-level circuits, and several ID/OOD settings.

The empirical accuracy–sparsity results are often strong. For example, Table 1 reports a 95% versus 83% ImageNet cACC while using 52% fewer components, and the majority-vote comparison in Figure 16 helps show that high-threshold selection contributes beyond simple ensembling.

The appendix includes useful analyses of sample complexity, runtime, larger radii, alternative component scorers, and random-seed stability. Family-wise error control is explicitly discussed in Appendix C.3.

The manuscript is well organized and visually clear. Its impact statement appropriately warns that certification is relative to a specific threat model and does not provide a complete explanation of model behavior.
weaknesses: The central theorem does not establish the claimed invariance of the three-valued circuit decision. Appendix A proves only that the unthresholded smoothed argmax satisfies A_tilde_u(D') = A_tilde_u(D). It never proves that the confidence at D' remains above tau, so the thresholded decision A_tilde^tau_u(D') may abstain. The final proof line silently equates these two different objects.

Even argmax stability for components decided at D does not imply that the certified-in set, and hence the circuit, remains unchanged after rediscovery on D'. Components that abstain at D are uncontrolled and may become certified-in at D'. Thus claims such as “the certified circuit remains unchanged” in the introduction, Theorem 3.1, Figure 2, and conclusion are materially stronger than the demonstrated one-sided partial-label guarantee.

The OOD evaluation involves substantial test-set selection. Appendix B.2 states that language certification hyperparameters are selected separately for each task/split by highest peak cACC, and Table 2 indeed uses different configurations for ID and OOD. Circuit size K is likewise chosen by peak accuracy on each evaluation dataset. This makes the reported OOD numbers optimistic and does not demonstrate deployment to an unseen shift with hyperparameters fixed using ID validation data.

The vision protocol is insufficiently clear and sometimes appears inconsistent. ID circuit discovery and evaluation use the same 50 ImageNet validation images per class. Appendix B.1 also says the same ImageNet classes are used for ImageNet-O, although standard ImageNet-O contains categories outside ImageNet-1k. The construction, label mapping, class intersections, and sample counts for each OOD benchmark need precise explanation.

The empirical results do not validate the advertised worst-case edit guarantee. There is no direct experiment that adversarially edits datasets within the certified radius and reruns the complete three-way procedure. Figure 6 instead examines distribution shifts outside the formal threat model and selects K at the point maximizing the certified–baseline accuracy gap, which risks selection bias.

The interpretation that abstained neurons are “spurious” or “actively harmful” is supported mainly by selected activation visualizations. Instability under random deletion does not itself establish spuriousness, semantic irrelevance, or causal harm; a systematic annotation or intervention study would be needed for these claims.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the displayed code link is empty, the selection-sample count n0 is not specified, relevance/activation/rank scoring implementations and K grids are underspecified, the sampled vision classes are not listed, and the exact paired significance test is not identified. Language results also lack uncertainty across datasets or seeds.

The combination of existing RS-Del and segmentation-style component certification is useful but technically incremental. Its significance depends heavily on the stronger circuit-invariance interpretation, which is precisely what the present proof does not support. The method could remain valuable after reframing it as certifying stable majority labels for selected components, but that would require substantial revision of the central claims and evaluation.
